title: {{NAME}} and the Princess Who Saved the Sky
moral: Real courage means choosing what is right over what is easy, especially when no one is watching.

pages.content:
The Kingdom of Aethon floated above the clouds like a thought too magnificent to descend. Its towers were made of something between stone and sky, the colour shifting from pale gold at dawn to deep rose in the afternoon. Bridges of woven light connected the islands that made up the kingdom, and below everything, where the clouds pulled apart, you could see the earth below, impossibly far and impossibly beautiful.

{{NAME}} had come by the sky-lift, a glass pod that rose from an unremarkable lamp-post in the ordinary world. He hadn't chosen to press the button. His hand had simply known.

Now he stood on the central island of the royal quarter, a cape billowing in a wind that smelled of high altitude and honey, watching the sky above the palace change colour in a way that had nothing to do with weather. Something was moving in the upper atmosphere. Something dark. Something that hadn't been there yesterday.

pages.content:
Princess Caelum had been monitoring the anomaly for six hours. She was the kingdom's chief sky-warden as well as its crown princess, which was a combination that suited her enormously.

She met {{NAME}} at the palace's observation deck with a terse handshake and the immediate sense that pleasantries had been suspended indefinitely. She was wearing a sky-warden's fitted indigo uniform with a golden circlet, and she was already talking before {{NAME}} had finished climbing the last step.

"The Fade is a weather entity," she said, pointing upward at a spreading darkness that looked like a bruise on the sky. "It consumes light energy. It grows. If it reaches the kingdom's anchor-crystal, the whole island structure will lose cohesion and everything held aloft by it will fall."

She turned to face {{NAME}} and studied him with the same intensity she'd been directing at the sky. "The sky-warden handbook has a solution. Chapter nine, page forty-seven. There's one problem." She paused. "It requires two people, and my partner injured both wrists yesterday."

"What does chapter nine say?" {{NAME}} asked.

pages.content:
Chapter nine required them to fly into the Fade itself.

Caelum handed {{NAME}} a sky-warden's harness and a pair of atmospheric gauntlets, gloves that projected focused beams of light energy. "The Fade can be split from within," she explained as they strapped in at the launch platform. "One person creates the anchor-point beam. The other keeps it stable while the other expands it outward from the centre. The Fade can't hold together if you break its core."

They launched into the dark with the exact feeling of jumping into cold water: a moment of pure, clear shock, and then the body's determination to move.

Inside the Fade was nothing like {{NAME}} had imagined. It wasn't dark. It was the absence of colour, a grey that felt like forgetting. It was cold and hushed, and it pressed against them from every direction. But Caelum moved through it with the utter steadiness of someone who had trained for this since she could walk.

"Anchor-point," she said, her voice sharp and clear in the grey silence. "Now, {{NAME}}."

He raised both gauntlets. A beam of white-gold blazed outward.

pages.content:
The Fade pushed back. It was, as it turned out, not simply a weather event. It was aware, and it did not want to be dispersed.

It pressed inward with a force that felt like every doubt {{NAME}} had ever had compressed into a single invisible weight. He felt his arms tremble. The beam flickered.

"Hold," Caelum said. Not commanding. Something better. Certain.

{{NAME}} looked at her. She was blazing. The light from her gauntlets was so intense it hurt to look at directly, and her expression was the most purely determined thing he had ever seen on a human face. She was not struggling. She was committed. There was a difference, and the difference was everything.

He straightened. He thought of the earth below, the bridges of light, the rose-gold towers. He thought of all the things held up by this sky.

He held.

The Fade fractured with a sound like an enormous window breaking very slowly. Colour returned to the world in a rush, amber and gold and vivid endless blue, and above them the sky was clear from horizon to horizon, wide open and blazing with late afternoon light.

pages.content:
They landed back on the observation deck to find half the kingdom had gathered there. A sound went up that was part cheer, part disbelief, and entirely warm.

Caelum stood very straight and acknowledged it with a single nod, which was more reserved than most people might manage after saving an entire floating kingdom. Then she turned to {{NAME}} and shook his hand again, the same terse handshake as before, except this time it was slower.

"Chapter nine also requires a debrief," she said. "Which takes approximately forty minutes and involves very good biscuits."

The biscuits were, in fact, extraordinary. They ate them on the observation deck as the kingdom's lights came on one by one below, tiny warm stars in the altitude dark. {{NAME}} was yawning by the time the sky-lift returned.

He was home and in bed before the ordinary world had noticed he'd gone. His violet cape hung on the chair. The silver crown emblem caught the glow of his bedside lamp and shone faintly.

He closed his eyes. The last thing he thought, before sleep took him completely, was that Caelum had slipped a small, folded page from the sky-warden handbook into his pocket. Chapter ten.
